📌 Clipboard Hijacking: Why the Address You Paste May Not Be Yours

Main Points
⏺ Crypto addresses are long, so almost everyone copies and pastes them
⏺ Clipboard malware watches for that moment and swaps in the attacker's address
⏺ This post explains how the swap works and the simple habit that stops it


1⃣ Core Idea — A clipper is malware that monitors your clipboard. When it sees something that looks like a wallet address, it silently replaces it with one controlled by the attacker.
2⃣ Why It Works — People check the first few and last few characters at most. Some clippers even pick look-alike addresses that match those characters.
3⃣ Example — You copy an exchange deposit address, paste it into your wallet, and hit send. The pasted address is different, and the transfer cannot be reversed.
4⃣ Risk Surface — Pirated software, fake wallet apps, cracked games and shady browser add-ons are common carriers. The malware can sit unnoticed for months.
5⃣ Practical Rule — After pasting, compare the full address with the source, or verify it on your hardware wallet screen. For new addresses, send a small test first.
Final Thoughts

The blockchain did exactly what you told it to do — the problem happened on your device before you clicked send. A ten-second check is cheaper than any lost transfer.

Nvidia Under Fire 📉

A growing national security controversy surrounding Nvidia is putting America's technology industry and the Trump administration under intense scrutiny.

The dispute centers on Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a company that reportedly purchased more than $4 billion worth of advanced Nvidia chips. U.S. authorities are investigating whether those semiconductors were illegally redirected to China, potentially violating American export restrictions.

Treasury Secretary Bessent publicly criticized Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the department's handling of the case. Bessent said Treasury, State and Defense officials had supported placing Megaspeed on an export-control list for months, but the Commerce Department had not taken the necessary action.

The controversy has become even more complicated following reports involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected Alice Huang of having connections to Chinese intelligence. These allegations have not been publicly established as proven facts, and China has denied the spying claims.

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive last week. Nvidia has said it cut off Megaspeed in June 2025 and blocked further orders and shipments. The company has denied facilitating illegal chip transfers.

The Justice Department is investigating whether export-control laws were violated. Members of Congress from both parties are demanding answers, with lawmakers calling for hearings and testimony from Commerce Department officials and Nvidia representatives.

The implications extend far beyond one company. Advanced AI chips are essential to artificial intelligence development, military applications and economic competitiveness. Washington has spent years trying to limit China's access to the most powerful American semiconductor technology.

The central question now is whether America's export-control system is strong enough to protect its technological advantage — and whether political or business relationships influenced decisions involving national security.

🌐 Former FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.47M in crypto from 35 investigations 

🔔 Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million in cryptocurrency through nearly 100 unauthorized transfers linked to 35 federal investigations. Yaroch, who previously worked in the bureau’s counterintelligence division, faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted his guilty plea in Alexandria, Virginia, with sentencing scheduled for March 4, 2027.

📊 Court documents show that Yaroch worked at the FBI’s Boston Division between 2017 and early 2025, where he was assigned to a squad investigating an adversarial nation-state. He subsequently transferred to the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division in February 2025, gaining access to FBI systems containing cryptocurrency credentials obtained during criminal and intelligence investigations. 

⚡️ Prosecutors said his thefts began no later than December 2024, before he moved to the new division. Using credentials associated with investigations outside his authorized activities, Yaroch accessed cryptocurrency wallets and transferred funds without permission. The approximately 100 fraudulent transactions involved credentials connected to 35 separate FBI investigations. Authorities calculated his total illicit proceeds at $2,474,380.66, substantially exceeding the roughly $1 million initially identified when his activities became public.

🇺🇸 AMERICA'S FIRST SILVER DOLLAR SOLD FOR $10 MILLION

On October 15, 1794, the Philadelphia Mint delivered 1,758 silver dollars, struck on a hand-turned screw press. It was the only day of dollar production that year.

These Flowing Hair dollars were the first silver dollars issued by the United States. Fewer than 200 are believed to survive.

The finest known example is unusual. A small silver plug was added to its blank at the Mint to bring it up to standard weight, and some experts believe it may be the very first silver dollar struck.

In 1947 the coin changed hands for $1,250. On January 24, 2013, at a Stack's Bowers Galleries auction in New York, it sold for $10,016,875. It was the first coin ever to top $10 million at auction.
